qs.q: An adult patient with AML presents with a very high white blood cell count (>70,000/uL) and develops cerebral and retinal hemorrhages. What is the immediate underlying pathophysiologic mechanism?
o: Leukostatic features caused by myeloid cells occluding microvasculature
Severe immune-mediated thrombocytopenic purpura in the vessels
Spontaneous bone marrow failure and extensive marrow infarction
Direct viral invasion of the central nervous system parenchyma
qs.e: AML patients with very high WBC counts (>70,000) can present with leukostatic features such as cerebral and retinal hemorrhage because myeloid cells occlude the microvasculature.

qs.q: A 54-year-old man evaluated for persistent fatigue has a normal total white blood cell count of 6,500/uL with a hemoglobin level of 11.2 g/dL. Which additional laboratory finding justifies obtaining a complete blood count with differential rather than just the total leukocyte count?
o: A hidden cell line abnormality masked by a normal total value
A technical limitation preventing automated total cell enumeration
An isolated alteration restricted strictly to erythrocyte indices
A direct mathematical correlation with mean corpuscular volume
qs.e: A normal total leukocyte count can mask significant shifts or cytopenias within specific subpopulations that only a differential reveals. The differential does not measure red cell indices or restrict evaluation solely to erythrocytes.

qs.q: A symptomatic 2-year-old girl undergoes a microscopic urinalysis evaluation. Which of the following white blood cell counts per high-power field is considered indicative of a urinary tract infection?
o: Fewer than two white blood cells
Greater than three white blood cells
Greater than fifty white blood cells
qs.e: A white blood cell count greater than 3-6 per high-power field strongly supports the diagnosis of a urinary tract infection in a symptomatic child. Normal children typically have very few or no white blood cells in their urine sediment.

qs.q: A 35-year-old male with chronic renal failure presents with severe lethargy and pallor. Laboratory results show a low red blood cell count. Which specific growth factor is primarily deficient in this patient?
qs.e: Erythropoietin (EPO) is of renal origin and triggers red blood cell production in response to hypoxia. Thrombopoietin regulates platelets, while G-CSF/GM-CSF drive granulocytes.

qs.q: An adult patient's differential white blood cell count shows a marked elevation of eosinophils. Which of the following conditions is most classically associated with this finding?
qs.e: Eosinophilia is strongly associated with parasitic infections and allergic reactions. Bacterial infections typically provoke a neutrophilia, while viral infections cause a lymphocytosis.
qs.s: Year 3: Haematology and Blood Transfusion Pathology: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with a chronic parasitic worm infestation is evaluated. Their differential white blood cell count shows a marked elevation of cells that typically participate in defense against parasites and allergic reactions. Which cell type is most likely increased?
qs.e: Eosinophils are granulocytes specialized in modulating allergic reactions and combating parasitic infections, making them the primary cell elevated in parasitic infestations. Neutrophils are instead the primary responders to acute bacterial challenges.

qs.q: A patient with suspected meningitis undergoes a lumbar puncture. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis shows turbid appearance, elevated white blood cell count with predominantly neutrophils, elevated protein, and decreased glucose. These findings are most consistent with:
qs.e: The described CSF findings (turbid, high neutrophils, high protein, low glucose) are characteristic of bacterial meningitis. Viral meningitis typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and normal glucose, while fungal and tuberculous meningitis have different patterns.

qs.q: An abnormal increase in red blood cell count is characterized by which of the following terms?
qs.e: Polycythemia refers to an abnormally high concentration of red blood cells in the blood.

ai.title: Complete Blood Cell Count in Children
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: A complete blood cell count (CBC) is a bedside tool that helps identify anaemia, infection, and marrow problems in children. Interpretation must consider age‑specific norms and common tropical diseases. In low‑resource settings, clinical correlation is essential when labs are limited.

sections.p: CBC measures haemoglobin, haematocrit, red cell indices, white cell count with differential and platelets. It is the first test when a child presents with fever, pallor, bruising or unexplained fatigue.
b: Provides quantitative data on all three cell lines
Requires only a small venous or capillary sample

t.a: Automated haematology analyser (or manual smear if machine unavailable)
t.b: What is the overall cellular picture? – Gives haemoglobin, WBC, platelet numbers and red cell indices; guides next diagnostic step

sections.p: Interpretation uses age‑specific reference ranges. Severe anaemia is defined as haemoglobin <7 g/dL in children <5 years and <8 g/dL in older children. Neutropenia is <1,500 cells/µL; severe neutropenia <500 cells/µL. Thrombocytopenia is <150,000/µL; severe <50,000/µL.
b: Mild, moderate, severe categories guide urgency of treatment
Combine CBC severity with clinical signs (e.g., tachycardia, bleeding) for staging

sections.p: In East African children the most common aetiologies differ by cell line.
b: Anaemia – nutritional iron deficiency, malaria, sickle cell disease, hookworm, chronic infection (TB, HIV)
Leukocytosis – bacterial sepsis, malaria, severe malaria, TB, acute schistosomiasis
Leukopenia – HIV, severe malaria, drug‑induced marrow suppression, aplastic crisis in sickle cell
Thrombocytopenia – malaria, dengue, HIV, sepsis‑associated DIC, herbal remedies

sections.p: Cell line abnormalities produce characteristic clinical pictures that help narrow the differential.
b: Anaemia – pallor, tachycardia, poor growth, dyspnoea on exertion
Leukocytosis – fever, rigors, focal infection, possible hepatosplenomegaly
Leukopenia – recurrent infections, oral thrush, weight loss
Thrombocytopenia – petechiae, bruising, mucosal bleeding, prolonged bleeding after minor trauma

sections.p: CBC is the gateway test; further work‑up is directed by the pattern seen.
b: Peripheral smear – morphology, malaria parasites, sickle cells
Reticulocyte count – marrow response in anaemia
Serology/PCR – HIV, malaria rapid test, TB GeneXpert when infection suspected

t.b: What is the morphology of red and white cells? – Detects malaria parasites, sickle cells, blasts; guides specific therapy
Is the marrow responding to anaemia? – High retic suggests peripheral loss (hemolysis, bleeding); low suggests marrow failure
Is malaria causing the cytopenia? – Positive test supports treatment; if unavailable, treat empirically in high‑risk area
Is HIV contributing to cytopenias? – Positive result prompts antiretroviral therapy and prophylaxis

sections.p: Certain CBC patterns signal life‑threatening conditions that need urgent action.
b: Severe anaemia with heart failure signs (tachycardia, hepatomegaly)
Neutropenia <500/µL with fever – risk of sepsis
Platelets <20,000/µL – spontaneous intracranial bleed risk
Leukocytosis >30,000/µL with blasts – possible acute leukaemia

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care based on the affected line.
b: Anaemia – iron supplementation for deficiency, antimalarial for malaria, transfusion for severe cases, hydroxyurea for sickle cell crises
Leukocytosis – appropriate antimicrobial (e.g., artesunate for severe malaria, broad‑spectrum antibiotics for bacterial sepsis)
Leukopenia – stop offending drugs, start cotrimoxazole prophylaxis in HIV, consider granulocyte colony‑stimulating factor if available
Thrombocytopenia – treat malaria or dengue, give platelet transfusion if <20,000/µL with bleeding, avoid NSAIDs

sections.p: Repeat CBC after treatment to confirm response and monitor for relapse.
b: Iron‑deficiency anaemia – repeat CBC in 4 weeks after iron therapy
Malaria‑related cytopenia – repeat CBC at 2 weeks to ensure recovery
Sickle cell – annual CBC and retic count; educate families on infection prevention
Anaemia vs. chronic heart disease – both cause tachycardia; CBC distinguishes by haemoglobin level
Leukocytosis vs. stress leukogram – infection shows left shift, stress leukogram shows mature neutrophilia

sections.p: Certain conditions mask true cell counts.
b: Severe dehydration concentrates cells, giving falsely high haemoglobin and haematocrit
Hemolysis in sample can lower haemoglobin and raise LDH, mimicking anaemia
Peripheral sequestration in malaria can cause transient neutropenia despite infection

whenToSeekHelp: Severe anaemia with respiratory distress or heart failure
Sudden drop in haemoglobin suggesting internal bleed

faq.q: Why is malaria a common cause of low platelets in children?
faq.a: Plasmodium parasites trigger immune‑mediated platelet destruction and sequestration in the spleen, leading to thrombocytopenia.

faq.q: Can a normal CBC rule out severe infection?
faq.a: No; early sepsis may have a normal or low white count, so clinical signs remain paramount.

faq.q: When should I transfuse a child with anaemia?
faq.a: When haemoglobin is <7 g/dL in children under 5 years (or <8 g/dL older) with signs of cardiac compromise or severe symptoms.

exam: A 4‑year‑old with fever, pallor and a haemoglobin of 6 g/dL – what immediate management steps and why? — Give oxygen, start urgent blood transfusion, investigate malaria and iron deficiency; explain that severe anaemia threatens cardiac output.

A child on antiretroviral therapy presents with neutrophils 400/µL and fever – what is your next action? — Treat as possible sepsis, obtain blood cultures, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, consider G‑CSF if available; highlight HIV‑related marrow suppression.

How does malaria‑induced thrombocytopenia differ from dengue‑related thrombocytopenia in presentation? — Malaria often has concurrent anaemia and splenomegaly; dengue shows high fever, rash and rapid platelet fall; both need supportive care but antimalarials vs. fluid management differ.
What red‑flag CBC finding would make you suspect acute leukaemia in a 7‑year‑old? — White cell count >30,000/µL with circulating blasts, anaemia and thrombocytopenia; requires bone‑marrow referral.
Why is iron supplementation contraindicated in a child with anaemia and a positive malaria test? — Iron can fuel parasite growth; treat malaria first, then give iron after parasite clearance.

A child with sickle cell disease has a reticulocyte count of 0.5 % and haemoglobin 5 g/dL – what does this indicate and how do you manage? — Low retic shows aplastic crisis; give urgent packed red cells and start antibiotics; avoid transfusion‑related alloimmunisation.

When is a platelet transfusion indicated in a paediatric patient with thrombocytopenia? — Platelets <20,000/µL with active bleeding or <10,000/µL even without bleeding; explain risk of intracranial haemorrhage.

How would you interpret a CBC that shows haemoglobin 11 g/dL, MCV 70 fL, and normal white count in a 3‑year‑old? — Microcytic, normochromic anaemia suggests iron deficiency; investigate diet, deworming, and malaria; start iron therapy.
